title: Labour sees off Green challenge to win Holborn by-election
summary: Labour's Sagal Abdi-Wali beats Green Party leader Zack Polanski to hold the north London seat.
body:
Labour's deputy leader Lucy Powell alongside Sagal Abdi-Wali following her by-election victory
Labour has won the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, seeing off a challenge from Green Party leader Zack Polanski.
Camden council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali held the north London seat for Labour, but the party's majority was reduced from 11,572 to 3,364.
At a victory rally, Abdi-Wali told supporters: "People voted for hope and now we're going to be able to deliver for them."
The by-election, which was triggered after former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer stood down as an MP, had been seen as a key test of whether Labour under Andy Burnham can win over voters who have switched to the Greens.
Speaking to BBC Breakfast after his defeat, Polanski said the result proved his party was "more of an electoral threat in these seats than we've ever been before".
"This is the foundation we're looking to build on," he added.
He insisted he would stay on as leader despite the result. Polanski is under pressure over his response to a policy motion passed by members at his party's conference that declared Zionism a form of racism.
MP Sagal Abdi-Wali makes housing her priority
Polanski vows to stay on as Green leader as criticism mounts
Chris Mason: Polanski faces greatest crisis of his leadership so far
Labour's Abdi-Wali secured 45% of the vote, followed by Polanski on 33%.
However, the Green Party's vote share was up by 22 percentage points on the 2024 general election.
The inner London constituency has been Labour since it was created in 1983, with the party taking at least 40% of the vote at every general election.
In her victory speech at the count in Camden, Abdi-Wali, who came to the UK as a child refugee from Somalia, said her victory was a testament to the success of diversity in the borough.
Later, speaking at a rally alongside Labour Party deputy leader Lucy Powell, she thanked voters for making her the MP "for this constituency that has given me so much".
"It gave me a community, gave me a home, gave me an opportunity, gave me an education, gave me so many of my friends - everything I am today has been shaped by it."
She told supporters that as an MP she would campaign on ending homelessness and taking Thames Water into public ownership.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham congratulated Abdi-Wali on a "fantastic campaign" while Burnham's predecessor Sir Keir said she was "a brilliant champion for our communities".
Asked what had gone wrong for his party, Polanski said the Greens had increased their vote share in the seat since the last election, describing the result as "our second best by-election result in Green Party history".
"I'm not going to sit here and pretend I'm not disappointed. No politician runs in a by-election and doesn't want to win," he told BBC Radio 4's Today.
"But at the same time, to see the growth in what was supposedly a safe Labour seat since 1983 [and] is now a marginal Labour seat, that's clearly growth and next time we can get it over the line."
Speaking to broadcasters earlier in the day, Polanski dismissed suggestions his leadership was under threat, saying: "Of course I can carry on as leader of the Green Party."
He said voters had been "excited about our plans for rent controls, tackling the climate crisis and nationalising Thames Water".
Sagal Abdi-Wali’s victory speech after by-election win
The Greens had hoped they could overturn Labour's substantial majority in the constituency after the party made gains in local elections in the area in May.
It saw a surge in support after Polanski took over as leader in September last year but in recent months polls suggest this has waned.
Earlier, former party leader Caroline Lucas told the BBC Polanski had failed to show leadership over the motion, passed by party members, which said Zionism was a form of racism.
Speaking after polls closed but before the result of the by-election was announced, Lucas criticised Polanski for not taking part in the debate or voting on the motion at the Green Party's conference in Brighton on Sunday, describing the motion as "dangerous" and "divisive".
Asked if Polanski should stand down, she said: "I think let's just see what happens in the coming days and weeks.
She continued: "I want him to speak now about what's happened, I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday.
"I think the jury is out about whether he will do that - but I very much hope he will."
The motion defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.
Polanski was not present for the vote on the motion, after leaving the conference early to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras.

title: Widdecombe suspect had 'particular hostility to Reform', court told
summary: Kerry is charged with the murder of the 78-year-old former Conservative minister and Reform UK spokeswoman.
body:
The man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe had a "particular hostility to Reform", prosecutors alleged on Friday.
They said Joshua Kerry, 28, "had an extreme left wing and/or anti-establishment mindset".
The prosecution also told the Old Bailey Widdecombe's murder had a "terrorist connection" as it was "politically and ideologically motivated".
Last week, Kerry, who had already been charged with Widdecombe's murder in July, was charged with a second offence of preparing terrorist acts.
He is accused of "online reconnaissance" of prominent people and institutions, travelling to Nigel Farage's home in South London on 19 April 2025, and trying to break into it 15 months before Widdecombe was killed.
Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb agreed to the prosecution request to join the two charges into one case.
The prosecution argued they were "inextricably linked".
Kerry appeared in court by video link from Belmarsh prison wearing a prison-issue grey sweatshirt.
The judge set a date for a five-week trial on 8 June next year.
The next hearing will be on 29 January.
Nicholas Lumley KC, defending, told the court that Kerry was likely to contest all the charges against him.
Kerry was charged in July with the murder of 78-year-old Widdecombe, a former Conservative minister and Reform spokeswoman.
Widdecombe was found dead on 9 July at her home in Haytor, Devon, having sustained serious injuries.
The former Tory MP was hit on the head with a hammer 21 times at her home as she ate lunch, prosecutors said during a hearing at Westminster Magistrates' Court in July.
She served as Conservative MP for Maidstone and the Weald in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.
She became a member of Reform in 2019.
Following her departure from the Commons, Widdecombe appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing in 2010 and was a runner-up on Celebrity Big Brother eight years later.

title: Chris Mason: Polanski faces greatest crisis of his leadership so far
summary: The Green leader faces pressure over his response to a party motion declaring Zionism a form of racism, as well as his by-election loss.
body:
In the aftermath of a by-election, the focus is usually on the winner. Not this time.
Make no mistake, the new MP for Holborn and St Pancras in north London, Sagal Abdi-Wali, has quite the story to tell.
She arrived in the UK as a child refugee from Somalia in the 1990s, grew up locally in Camden, became a councillor four years ago, the council leader in May and is now Sir Keir Starmer's successor as the MP.
But in the offices of Camden Council at three o'clock this morning, the focus of the press pack, me included, was on Zack Polanski, the leader of the Green Party of England and Wales, as we waited for the result.
This constituency has long been a safe Labour seat – the political home of the former prime minister and before that the former cabinet minister Frank Dobson. So a Labour victory here falls in the column marked "relief" for Downing Street rather than "jubilation".
Nonetheless, the Greens did very well in local elections in London in May, riding the crest of a political wave which began shortly after Polanski became the party's leader just over a year ago.
His failure to win here will prompt questions from some about stalling momentum, but the party can and does point to the big swing to them since the general election and a result that was by a long way the second best ever result for them at a Westminster by-election.
Incidentally, in finishing third the Conservatives have beaten Reform UK for the first time in an English by-election since the general election. It seems likely that Reform's result was hampered by Restore Britain, who managed almost half as many votes as Reform did, in a constituency not very favourable to either party.
Follow live updates: Labour wins Holborn and St Pancras by-election, beating Green leader Zack Polanski
Polanski defends leadership after Zionism row and by-election loss
But the real reason for the nocturnal scramble of cameras, microphones and questions for Polanski had little to do with the by-election – and everything to do with a vote at the Green Party's conference in Brighton last weekend.
Activists there passed a motion declaring Zionism as a form of racism.
The motion defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state" and backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.
Polanski didn't take part in the vote because, he said, he chose to campaign in Holborn and St Pancras instead. And he repeatedly declined to do interviews, as the pressure on him as ratcheted up.
But this morning he did speak to journalists.
He told BBC Breakfast that if he had he been there for the vote he "would have voted for the amendments".
Asked if he would have voted against the motion in the hall on that day, Polanski said: "the motion as amended I would have voted for, the motion unamended I wouldn't have voted for."
He added:  "I think it's an imperfect motion, there's parts I disagree with and parts I agree with."
Some in the party are furious about what has happened in recent days, with one figure telling me: "He has created a monster he either can't or won't control."
Green Party membership has increased more than three fold in the last year and internal critics of Polanski say this includes hard-left campaigners focused on the Middle East rather than environmental concerns.
Within the party and beyond it, a row is now boiling. Polanski, who is himself Jewish, has been banned from Israel. The Jewish Leadership Council and the Board of Deputies of British Jews have criticised the party, as have sister Green parties in Europe.
And – significantly – the former party leader and one of the most important figures in the Green movement of her generation, Caroline Lucas,told BBC Newsnight Polanski had failed to show leadership over the issue. She also failed to back him carrying on as leader.
Asked by reporters after the by-election result if he could continue as leader, Polanski insisted "of course I can carry on".
He did not explicitly reject the motion his party has passed, saying there was an "ongoing genocide and the displacement of the Palestinian people".
"I believe that is clearly racist," he added.
Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.
And asked if he believed in a two-state solution – an Israeli and Palestinian state existing peacefully alongside each other – he said "I believe it is not our role to decide".
He repeated that "it is my job to reassure people and make sure that we bring our party together".
"No one will be excluded in the Green Party based on faith and religion," he said.
But Polanski now confronts the greatest crisis of his leadership so far. He faces open, public insurrection about his judgement from senior figures internally and opprobrium from plenty of others beyond the party.
The campaign in Holborn and St Pancras might be over. The questions for Polanski certainly aren't.
